claims.text: The type and amount of X (Si, Mn, or Al) govern formation of a coherent, defect-engineered metal/oxide interface in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
An optimized X content promotes a slow-growing, adherent protective oxide scale.
The oxide scale produced at an optimized X content resists cracking and spallation above 900 °C.
The proposed alloys may initially be in either a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
Changing the type and concentration of X controls defect formation at the metal/oxide interface.
Changing the type and concentration of X can improve lattice matching at the metal/oxide interface.
Interfacial defect density and metal/oxide lattice matching mediate oxide-scale stability.
Element X promotes controlled formation of cation and oxygen vacancies.
Controlled cation and oxygen vacancy formation produces a gradual lattice-parameter transition between the metal substrate and growing oxide.
A gradual lattice-parameter transition reduces interfacial stresses during high-temperature exposure.
Reduced interfacial stress prevents oxide-scale cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNiX alloys with an optimized X level will form a slowly growing, coherent, and adherent protective oxide layer.
CrFeCoNiX alloys lacking optimal defect and lattice compatibility will exhibit rapid oxide growth.
CrFeCoNiX alloys lacking optimal defect and lattice compatibility will exhibit significant oxide cracking and spallation.
Earlier work identified a CrFeCoNiX baseline composition with sub-optimal X content that forms unstable, spalling oxide scales under high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies during prolonged exposure above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments.
Failure of adjusted-X alloys to improve interfacial coherence, defect matching, and resistance to cracking or spallation relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
